result:
**Verdicts: none of the three final answers is correct.** The true n₀ is at least 9.

**Solution 2 (answer 3):** It fails already at n = 4. The hypergraph with the single hyperedge V = {1,2,3,4} has δ₃ = 1, but it has only one edge, so it contains no Berge-C₄³.

**Solution 3 (answer 6):** The n = 6 claim is false. Take E₁ = {1,2,3,4}, E₂ = {1,2,5,6}, E₃ = {3,4,5,6}, plus the eight "transversal" triples (one vertex from each of {1,2}, {3,4}, {5,6}) as 3-edges. Every triple is covered, so δ₃ ≥ 1. Every 5-subset S = V∖{x} contains some Eᵢ, and S∖Eᵢ = {v}. In any 5-cycle on S, exactly two consecutive windows avoid v, and both lie inside Eᵢ. Triples inside Eᵢ are covered only by Eᵢ, so these two windows cannot receive distinct edges. Hence there is no Berge-C₅³ on 6 vertices.

**Solution 1 (answer 7):** The n = 7 claim is also false. Let F be the complements of the seven lines of the Fano plane (four-sets, pairwise meeting in 2 points), and add the seven Fano lines as 3-edges. Every triple is covered, and no triple inside a member of F lies in any other edge. Every pair of points lies on a line, so every 5-subset contains a member of F, and the same argument blocks every Berge-C₅³.

The same construction works for n = 8 using the 14 planes of AG(3,2), which form an SQS(8) in which each triple lies in exactly one edge. So n = 8 fails as well, and n₀ ≥ 9. The counting argument for exclusive four-sets suggests this obstruction disappears for n ≥ 9, so 9 is the likely value. I did not verify that the property holds for every n ≥ 9.

VERDICT 1: REJECT
VERDICT 2: REJECT
VERDICT 3: REJECT
